title: Majestic Trick
summary: Sacrifice the knight to place Black’s bishop where it will obstruct the king during the queen skewers.

nodes.question: Can White win instead of simply racing to promote?
nodes.explanation: The a-pawn is ready to advance, but Black’s bishop and d-pawn create tactical threats against Nc2. Taking b6 immediately only draws.

nodes.question: Why offer the knight on e3 with check?
nodes.explanation: The bishop on g5 can capture e3, but that new bishop square will later block the black king’s escape from a queen skewer.

branches.title: Lure the bishop before the queen race
commentary: Begin from the complete seven-piece source board. The selected ...Kf4 queen-checking route is encoded, not every king defense.
a6 advances the passer while keeping the knight available for a tactical offer.
Bg5+ checks Kf6 and moves the bishop away from the knight’s current lines.
Kg6 answers the check and approaches the squares needed to support the queen attack later.
d3 advances and attacks Nc2, forcing White to address the knight’s future.
Ne3+ offers the knight with check, deliberately inviting the bishop onto e3.
Bxe3 accepts the knight and places the bishop on the square that will obstruct its own king.
a7 continues the promotion race; the bishop can no longer stop this pawn.
d2 brings Black’s pawn one step from promotion as well.
a8=Q creates White’s queen first.
d1=Q creates Black’s queen. Despite the extra bishop and pawn, the exact position is winning for White.
Qg2+ begins the forcing checks, using Kg6 to restrict the black king’s route.
Kf4 is the source’s main king retreat.
Qg5+ keeps checking and prevents the king escaping toward f5.
Ke4 steps toward the bishop that was lured to e3.
Qf5+ drives the king toward the d-file. The e3 bishop occupies the escape square the king would otherwise want.
Kd4 is the illustrated move onto the queen’s file.
Qd7+ skewers Kd4 against Qd1, finally exploiting the bishop’s placement.
Kc3 answers the check but abandons the queen behind the king.
Qxd1 wins the queen. The exact queen-versus-bishop-and-pawn endpoint is winning for White; further conversion is outside this selected line.
branches.explanation: Qxd1 wins the queen. The exact queen-versus-bishop-and-pawn endpoint is winning for White; further conversion is outside this selected line.

branches.title: Take b6 and race without the lure
commentary: Compare the source’s immediate pawn capture instead of a6.
axb6 removes b6 but gives up the forced win.
Bg5+ checks the white king and gains time for the d-pawn race.
Kg6 answers the check while the knight remains on c2.
d3 starts Black’s run toward promotion.
b7 puts White’s passed pawn one step from its own promotion.
d2 leaves Black one step from promoting too.
b8=Q promotes, but without the bishop lure the exact position remains drawn.
d1=Q completes the source’s queen race. The tablebase confirms a draw with best play, rather than assuming equal queens always draw.
branches.explanation: d1=Q completes the source’s queen race. The tablebase confirms a draw with best play, rather than assuming equal queens always draw.

branches.title: Advance without the winning bishop lure
commentary: Compare the source’s rushed pawn line, whose stated losing result requires correction.
a7 gives up White’s forced win, but the exact result is a draw rather than a Black win.
dxc2 captures the knight and prepares promotion on c1. White still has an exact draw with correct play.
a8=Q promotes. The new queen preserves drawing resources despite Black’s extra bishop and pawn.
c1=Q completes the illustrated race. This exact position is drawn, correcting the source’s claim that Black is completely winning; the result is not inferred from material alone.
branches.explanation: c1=Q completes the illustrated race. This exact position is drawn, correcting the source’s claim that Black is completely winning; the result is not inferred from material alone.

exercises.prompt: Why is the bishop’s new square on e3 important?
exercises.answer: After Qg2+, Qg5+ and Qf5+, that bishop occupies e3, denying its king an escape and forcing it onto the d-file in front of Qd1.

exercises.prompt: Why does simply taking b6 not force a win?
exercises.answer: Both sides can promote without the e3 obstruction. The exact queen-race position is drawn with correct play.

startContext: The complete seven-piece source board is reconstructed visually. The a6 advance, Ne3+ bishop lure and selected ...Kf4 queen-skewer route are checked exactly, with the initial pawn-capture draw and rushed-pawn draw as comparisons. Other king routes remain source context.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.

sourceCorrections.claim: After a7 ...dxc2 a8=Q ...c1=Q, the source says White is completely losing.
sourceCorrections.correction: Every position in that four-ply line is exactly drawn. a7 gives up the forced win but does not lose with best play; the final queen/bishop/pawn material advantage is not an automatic win for Black.
